Derive the law of conservation of linear momentum, obtain the third law from it and solve recoil problems

slides.narration: A passenger lurches forward when the bus brakes. A fielder pulls the hands back while catching a fast ball. A rifle kicks back into the shoulder. All three follow from three laws of motion. In this part we study inertia, momentum, force as the rate of change of momentum, impulse, and the conservation of momentum, from which the third law follows.

slides.heading: Force and Newton’s first law
slides.body_md: A **force** is a push or a pull that changes, or tends to change, the state of rest or of uniform motion of a body, or its shape. **Newton’s first law:** every body continues in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless a net external force acts on it.
bullets: The law gives a **qualitative definition of force**: it is what changes the velocity of a body.
No net force means constant velocity: rest is just the special case of zero velocity.
On Earth a body does not go on for ever because friction and air drag are forces that act on it.
The law is also called the **law of inertia**.

rows: Net force is nearly zero, so the velocity does not change
A coin on a card over a glass, card flicked away
Coin drops straight into the glass
The coin stays at rest (inertia of rest) while the card leaves
Their bodies tend to keep moving (inertia of motion)
A cyclist on a straight road stops pedalling
Friction and drag are forces: they change the velocity

visual.alt: Table of situations showing the first law: a puck on ice, a coin on a card, a bus braking and a cyclist freewheeling, each with what happens and the reason

slides.narration: A force is a push or a pull that changes, or tends to change, the state of rest or of motion of a body. Newton’s first law says a body stays at rest or keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed unless a net external force acts on it. That gives us a qualitative idea of force. On Earth, friction and air drag are the forces that make moving bodies slow down.

slides.heading: Inertia and mass
slides.body_md: **Inertia** is the property of a body by which it resists any change in its state of rest or of uniform motion. Its measure is the **mass**: the greater the mass, the greater the inertia.
bullets: A loaded handcart is harder to start, and harder to stop, than an empty one: it has more mass, so more inertia.
**Inertia of rest:** passengers jerk backward when a train starts. **Inertia of motion:** they lurch forward when a bus brakes. **Inertia of direction:** they are thrown outward at a sharp turn.
Inertia is not a force; it is a property of matter. Mass is a scalar with SI unit kg.

rows: Passengers jerk backward when a train starts
The body tends to stay at rest while the floor moves forward
Passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes
The body tends to continue moving at the old velocity
Passengers are thrown outward at a sharp turn
The body tends to continue in a straight line

slides.narration: Inertia is the property of a body by which it resists a change in its state of rest or of uniform motion. Mass is the measure of inertia: a loaded handcart is harder to start or stop than an empty one. There is inertia of rest, as when a train starts and passengers jerk backward, inertia of motion, as when a bus brakes, and inertia of direction, as at a sharp turn.

slides.heading: Linear momentum
slides.body_md: The **linear momentum** of a body of mass $m$ moving with velocity $\vec{v}$ is $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$.
bullets: Momentum is a **vector**, in the direction of the velocity. SI unit: $\text{kg m s}^{-1}$, which is the same as $\text{N s}$; dimensions $[\text{M L T}^{-1}]$.
It measures how hard a body is to stop: a cricket ball and a car at one speed differ widely in momentum, and a fast light bullet can match a slow heavy body.
A change in momentum can come from a change in speed, in direction, or in both.

rows: A cricket ball, 0.16 kg at 30 m/s

visual.alt: Table of the momentum of a cricket ball, a sprinter, a bullet and a car, with mass and speed in each case

slides.narration: The linear momentum of a body is its mass times its velocity. It is a vector, pointing along the velocity, and its unit is kilogram metre per second, the same as newton second. The table shows how momentum differs widely between a cricket ball, a sprinter, a bullet and a car, which tells us how hard each one is to stop.

slides.heading: Newton’s second law: F = dp/dt
slides.body_md: The rate of change of momentum of a body is proportional to the net force on it, and takes place in the direction of the force. With the unit of force chosen so that the constant is $1$:
bullets: This is the general form. It holds even when the mass changes (a rocket burning fuel) and is the form that survives at speeds close to $c$.
The graph shows a trolley with a constant force of 6 N: the momentum rises by 6 kg m s⁻¹ every second, and the **slope of the $p$–$t$ graph is the force**.

visual.alt: Graph of momentum against time for a trolley acted on by a constant force of 6 newtons: a straight line from 4 kilogram metres per second whose slope of 6 kilogram metres per second per second is the force
visual.caption: The slope of the momentum–time graph is the force: F = dp/dt.

slides.narration: Newton’s second law says that the rate of change of momentum is proportional to the net force, and in the direction of the force. Choosing the unit of force suitably, force equals the rate of change of momentum. Over a short interval, the average force equals the change in momentum divided by the time. On a momentum time graph, the slope is the force.

slides.heading: F = ma as a special case
slides.body_md: For a body of **constant mass**, $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$ and the mass comes out of the derivative:
bullets: **One newton** is the force that gives a mass of $1$ kg an acceleration of $1\ \text{m s}^{-2}$: $1\ \text{N} = 1\ \text{kg m s}^{-2}$.
The vector equation splits into **component equations** along perpendicular axes; each is solved separately, so a force at an angle is resolved first.
For a fixed force, $a \propto 1/m$ (graph): a body with twice the mass has half the acceleration.

visual.alt: Graph of acceleration against mass for a fixed force of 12 newtons: a falling curve through 6 metres per second squared at 2 kilograms, 3 at 4 kilograms and 2 at 6 kilograms, showing that acceleration is inversely proportional to mass
visual.caption: For a fixed force the acceleration is inversely proportional to the mass.

math: \sum F_x = m a_x, \qquad \sum F_y = m a_y
slides.narration: If the mass is constant it comes out of the derivative, and force equals mass times acceleration. One newton is the force that gives a mass of one kilogram an acceleration of one metre per second squared. The vector equation can be split into components along two perpendicular axes, and each is solved on its own. For a fixed force, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the mass.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a crate pulled at an angle
slides.body_md: A crate of mass $40$ kg on a smooth floor is pulled by a rope with a force of $150$ N at $30^\circ$ above the horizontal. Take $g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$. Find the acceleration and the normal reaction.
bullets: Horizontal: $F\cos30^\circ = 130$ N, so $a = \dfrac{130}{40} = 3.25$ m s$^{-2}$.
Vertical: no acceleration, so $N + F\sin30^\circ = mg$.
$N = 392 - 75.0 = 317$ N, less than the weight because the rope lifts part of the load.

visual.alt: Table of the working for a crate pulled by a rope at 30 degrees: horizontal force, acceleration, vertical pull and normal reaction

slides.narration: Resolve the pull along the two axes. The horizontal part is one hundred and thirty newtons, so the acceleration is one hundred and thirty divided by forty, which is three point two five metres per second squared. Vertically the crate does not accelerate, so the normal reaction plus the vertical part of the pull equals the weight. The normal reaction is three hundred and seventeen newtons, less than the weight.

slides.heading: Mass near the speed of light (idea only)
slides.body_md: At everyday speeds mass is constant and $F = ma$ works. As the speed of a body approaches the speed of light $c$, experiments show that its **measured mass increases** and tends to infinity.
bullets: At 0.100 c the increase is only 0.50 per cent; at 0.900 c the mass is 2.29 times the rest mass; at 0.990 c it is 7.09 times.
So no material body can be accelerated to the speed of light, however long a force acts.
Here $F = ma$ with a fixed $m$ fails, but $F = \dfrac{dp}{dt}$ still holds: this is why the second law is stated through momentum. Only the idea is required; no calculation.

x.label: speed v as a fraction of c

visual.alt: Graph of measured mass over rest mass against speed as a fraction of the speed of light: almost flat up to about a tenth of the speed of light, then rising steeply, about 1.25 at 0.6, 2.3 at 0.9 and 7.1 at 0.99, growing without limit as the speed approaches the speed of light
visual.caption: Mass seems to grow as v approaches c; at everyday speeds the change is negligible.

slides.narration: At everyday speeds the mass of a body is constant. As the speed approaches the speed of light, experiments show that the measured mass increases, without limit. So a force cannot push a body to the speed of light. In that region force equals mass times acceleration, with a fixed mass, fails, but force equals the rate of change of momentum still holds. We need only the idea.

slides.heading: Impulse
slides.body_md: **Impulse** is the product of a force and the time for which it acts. For a force that varies, it is the **area under the force–time graph**.
bullets: It follows from $F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$: impulse equals the **change in momentum**. Unit $\text{N s} = \text{kg m s}^{-1}$; vector, along the change in momentum.
The bat in the figure acts on a 0.15 kg ball for 0.005 s: a peak of 3000 N but an average of 1500 N; the impulse 7.5 N s is the area.
For a bounce back, take directions into account: a ball arriving at $u$ and leaving at $v$ the other way has $\Delta p = m(v + u)$.

In the figure the bat acts on the ball for zero point zero zero five seconds. The peak force is three thousand newtons, the average is one thousand five hundred newtons, and the impulse is seven point five newton seconds. When a ball bounces back, add the two speeds.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: catching a ball
slides.body_md: A fielder catches a cricket ball of mass $0.16$ kg moving at $28$ m s$^{-1}$. Find the average force on the hands if the ball is stopped in (i) $0.02$ s with rigid hands, (ii) $0.08$ s by drawing the hands back.
bullets: Impulse $= \Delta p = m v = 0.16 \times 28 = 4.48$ N s in both cases.
(i) $F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{4.48}{0.02} = 224$ N.
(ii) $F = \dfrac{4.48}{0.08} = 56.0$ N, **one quarter** of the first, because the time is four times as long.

visual.alt: Table comparing the average stopping force for a catch with rigid hands over 0.02 seconds and with hands drawn back over 0.08 seconds, with the same impulse

slides.narration: The impulse needed to stop the ball is its momentum, four point four eight newton seconds, whichever way it is stopped. With rigid hands the stopping time is zero point zero two seconds and the average force is two hundred and twenty four newtons. Drawing the hands back makes the time zero point zero eight seconds, so the force falls to fifty six newtons. A longer time means a smaller force for the same impulse.

slides.heading: Conservation of linear momentum
slides.body_md: For a system of bodies, Newton’s second law reads: net **external** force $= \dfrac{d\vec{P}}{dt}$, where $\vec{P}$ is the total momentum. For an **isolated system** the external force is zero:
bullets: **Law:** the total linear momentum of an isolated system stays constant; whatever one part gains, another loses.
It is a vector law: it holds for each component separately, with signs for directions.
Internal forces (collisions, explosions, recoil) change the momenta of the parts but not the total. The law is confirmed in all experiments and holds even where it is hard to use the forces.

rows: m₁ v₁ + m₂ v₂ (the same total)

visual.alt: Table of conservation of momentum for a gun and bullet, a collision of two bodies and an exploding bomb, giving the total momentum before and after

slides.narration: For a system of bodies, the net external force equals the rate of change of the total momentum. For an isolated system there is no external force, so the total momentum does not change. That is the law of conservation of linear momentum. It is a vector law. Internal forces, as in collisions and explosions, can shift momentum from one part to another but cannot change the total.

slides.heading: The third law follows from conservation
slides.body_md: Take two bodies A and B that interact only with each other, an isolated pair. Conservation of momentum gives $\vec{p}_A + \vec{p}_B = \text{constant}$.
bullets: **Newton’s third law:** to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. The force on A by B is equal and opposite to the force on B by A.
The two forces act at the **same time** on **different bodies**, so they never cancel each other; each produces its own acceleration.
In the figure the forces are equal (50 N), but the lighter skater accelerates more, $a = F/m$.

slides.narration: Take two bodies that interact only with each other. Their total momentum is constant, so the rate of change of one momentum is minus the rate of change of the other. Therefore the force on A equals minus the force on B. This is the third law: action and reaction are equal and opposite. They act on different bodies, so they do not cancel, and the lighter skater accelerates more.

slides.heading: Recoil of a gun
slides.body_md: A gun of mass $M$ fires a bullet of mass $m$ at velocity $\vec{v}$. Before firing the total momentum is zero. After firing:
bullets: The minus sign: the gun **recoils** in the opposite direction. The two momenta are equal in size and opposite.
Because $M \gg m$, the recoil speed is small; here $V = 2$ m s⁻¹ against $v = 400$ m s⁻¹.
The kinetic energies are **not** equal: $\dfrac{K_{\text{gun}}}{K_{\text{bullet}}} = \dfrac{m}{M}$, so the light bullet carries nearly all the energy.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 1
slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: No net force: rest or uniform motion; inertia measured by mass
p = m v, vector, kg m/s
F = dp/dt; F = ma for constant mass; 1 N = 1 kg m/s²
J = F Δt = Δp = area under the F–t graph
From conservation: forces of a pair equal and opposite, on different bodies
V = − m v / M; momenta equal and opposite

visual.alt: Summary table of the first law, momentum, the second law, impulse, conservation of momentum, the third law and recoil

slides.narration: To sum up. With no net force a body keeps its velocity, and inertia is measured by mass. Momentum is mass times velocity. Force is the rate of change of momentum, and for constant mass it is mass times acceleration. Impulse is force times time and equals the change in momentum. In an isolated system the total momentum is conserved, which gives the third law and explains recoil.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 1
bullets: Give the law, then the formula, then the working: marks are given for each. In F = dp/dt, say that the force is the **net** force.
Derivations: F = ma (take $m$ constant out of the derivative); conservation of momentum (no external force, so $dP/dt = 0$); third law from conservation (differentiate $p_A + p_B$).

Common mistakes: treating action and reaction as acting on one body so that they cancel; forgetting the direction (sign) of velocities in a rebound or recoil; calling inertia a force; using grams for mass in newtons.
State the condition for conservation: no external force (or negligible during the short interaction).

slides.narration: In the examination, give the law, the formula and then the working. Say that the force is the net force. Learn the derivations: force equals mass times acceleration from the rate of change of momentum, conservation of momentum, and the third law from conservation. Common mistakes are letting action and reaction cancel, forgetting signs in rebound and recoil, and using grams instead of kilograms.

slides.narration: How fast does a block slide when a hanging mass pulls it over the edge of a table? What does a weighing machine read inside a lift? How steeply can a ladder lean on a smooth wall? Each problem is solved the same way: draw a free body diagram for each body, then apply the laws of motion. In this part we do that for connected bodies and for forces in equilibrium.

slides.heading: Free-body diagrams: weight, normal reaction and tension
slides.body_md: A **free-body diagram** (FBD) isolates one body, or part of a system, and shows **only the forces acting on it**, each as an arrow from the body, with the axes marked.
bullets: **Weight** $mg$ acts down. The **normal reaction** $N$ is perpendicular to the surface of contact and pushes the body away from it; it adjusts to whatever value is needed (it is not always $mg$).
**Tension** $T$ pulls along a string, away from the body. For a light string over a smooth pulley the tension is the **same throughout** the string.
Do not draw forces that the body exerts on others, and do not draw “resultant” or “force down the slope” as an extra force: components are drawn dashed.
Then write $\sum F = ma$ for each body along each axis.

rows: Perpendicular to the surface, away from it
Away from the body, along the string

visual.alt: Table of the forces drawn in a free-body diagram: weight, normal reaction, tension and applied force, with where each acts and its direction

slides.narration: A free body diagram shows one body on its own, with only the forces acting on it. Weight acts downward. The normal reaction is perpendicular to the surface and adjusts itself, so it is not always equal to the weight. Tension acts along a string, and for a light string over a smooth pulley it is the same everywhere. Then write force equals mass times acceleration for each body.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a block on a smooth incline
slides.body_md: A block of mass $6$ kg slides on a smooth plane inclined at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal. Take $g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$. Find the normal reaction and the acceleration.
bullets: Forces: weight $mg = 58.8$ N down, and $N$ perpendicular to the plane. Take axes along and perpendicular to the plane.
Perpendicular (no acceleration): $N = mg\cos30^\circ = 50.9$ N.
Along the plane: $mg\sin30^\circ = ma$, so $a = g\sin30^\circ = 4.90$ m s$^{-2}$ down the slope, whatever the mass.

slides.heading: The Atwood machine (one pulley)
slides.body_md: Masses $m_1 > m_2$ hang from a light string over a smooth pulley. $m_1$ goes down and $m_2$ goes up with the same acceleration $a$.
bullets: Adding the two equations gives $a$; substituting back gives $T$. If $m_1 = m_2$, then $a = 0$ and $T = mg$.
$T$ lies between the two weights: $m_2 g < T < m_1 g$. (Problems with two pulleys are not required.)
The same method works for any chain of bodies joined by light strings.

bullets: Treat both as one body to find $a$; then isolate B: the only horizontal force on B is the contact force $F_c$ from A.
A feels $F_c$ backward from B: a third-law pair, equal and opposite. For A: $F - F_c = m_1 a$.

slides.heading: A lift: apparent weight
slides.body_md: A person of mass $m$ stands on a weighing machine in a lift of upward acceleration $a$. The machine reads the normal reaction $N$ (the **apparent weight**). Taking upward as positive: $N - mg = ma$.
bullets: Upward acceleration, or slowing down while moving down, makes $N > mg$: you feel heavier. Downward acceleration makes $N < mg$: you feel lighter.
Constant velocity, up or down, gives the true weight. If the cable snaps, $a = g$ and $N = 0$: **weightlessness**.
For 60 kg and $a = 1.5$ m s⁻² the readings are 678 N, 588 N and 498 N.

slides.heading: Equilibrium of concurrent forces
slides.body_md: Forces whose lines of action meet at a point are **concurrent**. A body is in **equilibrium** when the resultant is zero, $\sum\vec{F} = 0$.
bullets: **Triangle law:** if three forces keep a particle in equilibrium, they can be drawn head to tail to form a **closed triangle**. For more forces the closed figure is a **polygon**.
**Parallelogram law:** the resultant of two forces is the diagonal of the parallelogram on them; in equilibrium the third force is equal and opposite to that diagonal.
**Resolution:** equivalently, resolve along two perpendicular axes: $\sum F_x = 0$ and $\sum F_y = 0$.
The lamp in the figure is held by two strings: the weight, $T_2$ and $T_1$ close the triangle.

slides.narration: Forces whose lines of action meet at a point are concurrent. For equilibrium their resultant is zero. By the triangle law, three forces in equilibrium can be drawn head to tail to form a closed triangle. By the parallelogram law, the resultant of two forces is the diagonal of the parallelogram, and the third force is equal and opposite to it. Or resolve along two axes and set each sum to zero.

slides.heading: Resolution and Lami’s theorem
slides.body_md: **Lami’s theorem:** if three concurrent forces are in equilibrium, each is proportional to the sine of the angle between the other two.
bullets: It is the sine rule applied to the closed force triangle: each side is a force, and the angle opposite a side is the **supplement** of the angle between the other two forces.
For a lamp of weight $W$ on strings at $\alpha$ (left) and $\beta$ (right) to the horizontal: $T_1 = \dfrac{W\cos\beta}{\sin(\alpha + \beta)}$ and $T_2 = \dfrac{W\cos\alpha}{\sin(\alpha + \beta)}$.
Resolving horizontally and vertically gives the same answers; use whichever method is quicker.

visual.alt: Table comparing the two methods for the lamp on two strings: resolving along two directions and Lami’s theorem, giving 38.7 and 49.3 newtons

slides.narration: Lami’s theorem says that if three concurrent forces are in equilibrium, each force is proportional to the sine of the angle between the other two. It is just the sine rule applied to the closed force triangle. For a lamp on two strings, it gives each tension directly. Resolving horizontally and vertically gives the same answers, so use whichever method is quicker.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a lamp on two strings
slides.body_md: A lamp of weight $60$ N hangs from a knot held by two strings making $35^\circ$ (left) and $50^\circ$ (right) with the horizontal ceiling. Find the tensions.
bullets: The angle between the strings is $180^\circ - (35^\circ + 50^\circ) = 95^\circ$, and $\sin85^\circ = 0.9962$.
Lami: $T_1 = \dfrac{60\cos50^\circ}{\sin85^\circ} = 38.7$ N.
$T_2 = \dfrac{60\cos35^\circ}{\sin85^\circ} = 49.3$ N.
Check by resolving horizontally: $T_1\cos35^\circ = 31.7$ N $= T_2\cos50^\circ = 31.7$ N.

slides.heading: Three coplanar forces on a rigid body
slides.body_md: For a **rigid body** two conditions must hold, not one: no net force **and** no net torque.
bullets: **Translation:** $\sum\vec{F} = 0$. **Rotation:** the sum of torques about any point is zero.

**Three non-parallel coplanar forces** can keep a rigid body in equilibrium only if their **lines of action meet at one point**. If they met at no common point, the torque about the meeting point of two of them would be due to the third alone, and could not vanish.
Three **parallel** forces are also possible: the middle force acts opposite to the other two (like a plank on two supports).
This gives a graphical method: find where two lines of action meet, then the third line must pass through that point.

rows: No acceleration of the centre of mass (translation equilibrium)
Sum of torques about any point = 0
Their lines of action must meet at one point
Possible, with the middle force opposite to the other two

slides.narration: A rigid body needs two conditions for equilibrium: no net force and no net torque. If three forces in one plane are not parallel and keep a rigid body in equilibrium, their lines of action must meet at one point. Otherwise the third force would give a torque about the meeting point of the other two. Three parallel forces are also possible, with the middle one opposite to the other two.

slides.heading: The ladder against a smooth wall
slides.body_md: A uniform ladder of length $L$ and weight $W$ makes an angle $\theta$ with the floor and leans on a **smooth** wall. A smooth wall exerts only a **horizontal** reaction $N_w$ (perpendicular to it).
bullets: At the floor there are two reaction components: a vertical $N_f$, and a horizontal force $F_f$ (taken here simply as the reaction component found from equilibrium; its limit comes with friction in the next chapter).
Vertical balance gives $N_f$; horizontal balance gives $F_f = N_w$; torques about the foot give $N_w$ (the floor forces have no torque about the foot).
The three lines of action meet at **Q**, above the middle of the ladder: floor reaction $\tan\phi = N_f/F_f = 2\tan\theta$ with the floor.
A less steep ladder (smaller $\theta$) needs a larger $N_w$ and a larger horizontal force at the floor.

slides.narration: To sum up. Draw a free body diagram for each body, and apply force equals mass times acceleration along each axis. Connected bodies share the same acceleration and, over a light string and smooth pulley, the same tension. In a lift, the scale reads m times g plus or minus a. Concurrent forces in equilibrium form a closed triangle, and Lami’s theorem applies. For a rigid body, forces and torques both vanish.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 2
bullets: Draw a **separate FBD for each body** and label every force; marks are given for the diagram. Do not show the resultant as an extra force, and do not forget the normal reaction.
Choose the positive direction in the direction of motion for each body, and say so. The acceleration and the tension are the **same magnitude** for bodies on one light string.

Lift: write $N - mg = ma$ with a sign for $a$; check that $N > mg$ when accelerating up. Ladder: take torques about the foot (the unknown floor forces drop out), and give the direction of each reaction.

Common mistakes: using $T = mg$ when the body accelerates; adding the weights in the Atwood machine; treating the wall reaction as vertical; giving the angle of Lami’s theorem as the angle between the strings rather than its sine.

sections.heading: 1. Force and inertia; Newton’s first law
sections.body_md:
- A **force** is a push or a pull that changes, or tends to change, the state of rest or of uniform motion of a body, or its shape.
- **First law (law of inertia):** a body continues in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless a net external force acts on it. It gives the qualitative meaning of force.
- **Inertia** is the property by which a body resists a change in its state of rest or of uniform motion; **mass** is its measure. A larger mass means a larger inertia.
- Kinds: inertia of **rest** (passengers jerk backward when a train starts), of **motion** (passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes), of **direction** (thrown outward at a sharp turn).
- Inertia is a property, not a force. Friction and air drag are the forces that make bodies on Earth come to rest.

sections.heading: 2. Momentum; the second law F = dp/dt and F = ma; mass near the speed of light
sections.body_md:
- **Linear momentum** $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$: a vector along $\vec{v}$; SI unit kg m s⁻¹ (= N s); dimensions [M L T⁻¹].
- **Second law:** the rate of change of momentum is proportional to the net force and takes place along it: $\vec{F} = \dfrac{d\vec{p}}{dt}$. The average force over $\Delta t$ is $\Delta\vec{p}/\Delta t$.
- For **constant mass**, $\vec{F} = m\dfrac{d\vec{v}}{dt} = m\vec{a}$. One **newton** is the force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s⁻²: 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻².
- **Components:** $\sum F_x = ma_x$ and $\sum F_y = ma_y$, solved separately. Example: a 40 kg crate pulled by 150 N at 30° on a smooth floor has $a = 3.25$ m s⁻² and $N = 317$ N.
- **Idea only:** as v approaches c the measured mass increases without limit, so no body can reach c; F = ma with constant m fails there, but F = dp/dt still holds.

The force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s⁻².

sections.heading: 3. Impulse; conservation of linear momentum; the third law; recoil
sections.body_md:
- **Impulse** $\vec{J} = \vec{F}\Delta t = \Delta\vec{p}$ (average force); for a varying force it is the **area under the F–t graph**. Unit N s = kg m s⁻¹. A long stopping time means a small force: catching a 0.16 kg ball at 28 m s⁻¹ needs 4.48 N s, giving 224 N in 0.02 s but 56.0 N in 0.08 s.
- **Conservation of momentum:** for an isolated system the net external force is zero, so $d\vec{P}/dt = 0$ and the total momentum is constant: $m_1u_1 + m_2u_2 = m_1v_1 + m_2v_2$ (along a line, with signs).
- **Third law from conservation:** for two bodies interacting only with each other, $d\vec{p}_A/dt + d\vec{p}_B/dt = 0$, so the force on A is equal and opposite to the force on B. The forces act on **different bodies** at the same time and do not cancel.
- **Recoil:** from rest, $0 = mv + MV$, so $V = -mv/M$; the momenta are equal and opposite while the kinetic energies are in the ratio $m : M$. A 3.6 kg rifle firing 0.012 kg at 750 m s⁻¹ recoils at 2.50 m s⁻¹. For the gun in the figure V = 2 m s⁻¹.

sections.heading: 4. Free-body diagrams, tension, normal reaction; connected bodies
sections.body_md:
- A **free-body diagram** shows one body and only the forces on it: weight $mg$ down, **normal reaction** $N$ perpendicular to the surface, **tension** $T$ along a string, applied forces. Then $\sum F = ma$ along each axis.
- A light string over a smooth pulley has the same tension throughout. Bodies on one string have the same acceleration.
- **Smooth incline:** $N = mg\cos\theta$, $a = g\sin\theta$ (for 6 kg at 30°: $N = 50.9$ N, $a = 4.90$ m s⁻²).
- **Table and hanging mass:** $a = \dfrac{m_2g}{m_1 + m_2}$, $T = \dfrac{m_1m_2g}{m_1 + m_2}$ (3 kg and 2 kg: 3.92 m s⁻², 11.8 N).
- **Atwood machine (one pulley):** $a = \dfrac{(m_1 - m_2)g}{m_1 + m_2}$, $T = \dfrac{2m_1m_2g}{m_1 + m_2}$ (5 kg and 3 kg: 2.45 m s⁻², 36.75 N). Two-pulley systems are not required.
- **Blocks in contact:** $a = F/(m_1 + m_2)$ and contact force $m_2a$ (here 6.00 N).
- **Lift:** $N = m(g \pm a)$; $+$ accelerating up, $-$ accelerating down; zero when the cable snaps (60 kg: 678 N, 588 N, 498 N).

key_terms.definition_md: A diagram of one body showing only the forces acting on it.
The contact force perpendicular to a surface; it adjusts to what is needed.
The pull along a string; the same throughout a light string over a smooth pulley.
The normal reaction on a body in an accelerating frame, as read by a weighing machine.

sections.heading: 5. Equilibrium of concurrent forces; three coplanar forces on a rigid body; the ladder
sections.body_md:
- **Concurrent forces** in equilibrium: $\sum\vec{F} = 0$. **Triangle law:** three such forces drawn head to tail close a triangle (a polygon for more). **Parallelogram law:** the third force is equal and opposite to the diagonal of the parallelogram on the other two. **Resolution:** $\sum F_x = 0$, $\sum F_y = 0$.
- **Lami’s theorem:** each force is proportional to the sine of the angle between the other two. A lamp of 60 N on strings at 35° and 50° to the ceiling: $T_1 = 38.7$ N, $T_2 = 49.3$ N.
- **Rigid body:** $\sum\vec{F} = 0$ and the sum of torques about any point $= 0$. Three non-parallel coplanar forces keep it in equilibrium only if their lines of action meet at one point; three parallel forces need the middle one opposite to the others.
- **Ladder** (length $L$, weight $W$, angle $\theta$, smooth wall): $N_f = W$, $F_f = N_w$, torques about the foot give $N_w = \dfrac{W}{2}\cot\theta$. A 6 m ladder of 20 kg at 50°: $N_w = F_f = 82.2$ N, $N_f = 196$ N. The floor horizontal force is just a reaction component found from equilibrium; its limit comes with friction.

key_terms.definition_md: Forces whose lines of action meet at a point.
For three concurrent forces in equilibrium, each is proportional to the sine of the angle between the other two.
The turning effect of a force about a point; force times perpendicular distance.
A wall that exerts only a reaction perpendicular to itself.

notes.exam_tips_md:
- Law, formula, working, units: each earns marks. In F = dp/dt the force is the net force; for F = ma the mass is constant.
- Derivations to learn: F = ma from F = dp/dt; conservation of momentum (no external force); the third law from conservation; the Atwood machine; N = m(g ± a) in a lift; Lami's theorem; N_w = (W/2) cot θ for the ladder.
- Draw a separate free-body diagram for each body and mark the positive direction. Tension and acceleration are the same for bodies on one light string.
- Action and reaction act on different bodies, so they never cancel; weight and the normal reaction are not such a pair.
- Give signs to velocities in rebound and recoil problems. Use kg and m s⁻¹ (not grams) in newton calculations.
- Ladder: take torques about the foot; the wall reaction is horizontal for a smooth wall.

cards.front_md: State Newton’s first law.
cards.back_md: A body stays at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless a net external force acts on it.

cards.front_md: What is inertia, and what measures it?
cards.back_md: The property of resisting a change in the state of rest or uniform motion; it is measured by mass.

cards.front_md: Name the three kinds of inertia.
cards.back_md: Of rest, of motion and of direction.

cards.front_md: Why do standing passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes?
cards.back_md: Their bodies tend to keep moving at the old velocity (inertia of motion) while the bus slows.

cards.front_md: Define linear momentum. Unit?
cards.back_md: $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$, a vector; kg m s⁻¹ (equal to N s).

cards.front_md: Write Newton’s second law in its general form.
cards.back_md: $\vec{F} = \dfrac{d\vec{p}}{dt}$: the net force equals the rate of change of momentum.

cards.front_md: How does F = ma follow from F = dp/dt?
cards.back_md: For constant mass, $\dfrac{d(m\vec{v})}{dt} = m\dfrac{d\vec{v}}{dt} = m\vec{a}$.

cards.front_md: Define the newton.
cards.back_md: The force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s⁻²; 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻².

cards.front_md: How is $\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$ used with components?
cards.back_md: Resolve forces along two perpendicular axes: $\sum F_x = ma_x$ and $\sum F_y = ma_y$, solved separately.

cards.front_md: What does the slope of a momentum–time graph give?
cards.back_md: The net force on the body.

cards.front_md: What happens to the measured mass of a particle as v approaches c? (idea only)
cards.back_md: It increases without limit, so no body can reach c; F = dp/dt still holds.

cards.front_md: Define impulse. Unit?
cards.back_md: $\vec{J} = \vec{F}\Delta t = \Delta\vec{p}$; N s (= kg m s⁻¹). For a varying force, the area under the F–t graph.

cards.front_md: Why does a fielder draw the hands back while catching?
cards.back_md: The change in momentum is fixed; a longer stopping time gives a smaller average force.

cards.front_md: State the law of conservation of linear momentum.
cards.back_md: The total linear momentum of an isolated system (no net external force) stays constant.

cards.front_md: Write conservation of momentum for two bodies in a line.
cards.back_md: $m_1u_1 + m_2u_2 = m_1v_1 + m_2v_2$, with signs for directions.

cards.front_md: How does the third law follow from conservation of momentum?
cards.back_md: For two bodies alone, $dp_A/dt + dp_B/dt = 0$, so the force on A is equal and opposite to the force on B.

cards.front_md: Why do action and reaction not cancel each other?
cards.back_md: They act on different bodies.

cards.front_md: Recoil velocity of a gun from rest?
cards.back_md: $V = -\dfrac{m}{M}v$: opposite to the bullet; momenta equal and opposite.

cards.front_md: What is a free-body diagram?
cards.back_md: A diagram of one body showing only the forces acting on it.

cards.front_md: Direction of the normal reaction?
cards.back_md: Perpendicular to the surface of contact, away from the surface; it adjusts to what is needed.

cards.front_md: What is true about the tension in a light string over a smooth pulley?
cards.back_md: It is the same throughout the string.

cards.front_md: Acceleration of a block on a smooth incline of angle θ?
cards.back_md: $a = g\sin\theta$ down the slope, with $N = mg\cos\theta$.

cards.front_md: Atwood machine: acceleration and tension?
Block $m_1$ on a smooth table, $m_2$ hanging: $a$ and $T$?
Contact force between blocks $m_1$ (pushed by F) and $m_2$ ahead of it?
Reading of a weighing machine in a lift accelerating up at a?
cards.back_md: $N = m(g + a)$; downward acceleration gives $m(g - a)$; free fall gives 0.

cards.front_md: State the triangle law for forces in equilibrium.
cards.back_md: Three concurrent forces in equilibrium can be drawn head to tail as a closed triangle.

cards.front_md: State Lami’s theorem.
cards.back_md: For three concurrent forces in equilibrium, each is proportional to the sine of the angle between the other two.

cards.front_md: Conditions for equilibrium of three coplanar forces on a rigid body?
cards.back_md: Zero resultant force and zero torque; if not parallel, their lines of action meet at one point.

cards.front_md: Wall reaction for a uniform ladder at angle θ on a smooth wall?
cards.back_md: $N_w = \dfrac{W}{2}\cot\theta$ (torques about the foot), with $F_f = N_w$ and $N_f = W$.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A city bus is moving steadily when the driver applies the brakes hard. Standing passengers lurch forward because

options.text_md: the brakes exert a forward force on the passengers as they slow the bus down
a forward force acts on a body whenever it is inside a vehicle that is slowing down
the weight of the passengers shifts forward when the bus slows down suddenly
their bodies tend to keep moving forward at the old velocity while the bus slows down

questions.solution_md: By the first law a body keeps its state of uniform motion unless a net force acts on it. The bus is slowed by the brakes, but the passengers, who are not held by the bus, tend to continue at the old velocity: inertia of motion. No forward force pushes them.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (d)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: Of the following, the quantity that measures the inertia of a body is its

options.text_md: weight at the place where it is measured

questions.solution_md: Inertia is the resistance of a body to a change in its state of rest or of uniform motion. Its measure is the mass, which does not change from place to place, unlike weight.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (a)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A ropeway cabin full of passengers is going up a hillside at a steady 3 m s⁻¹ along a straight cable. The total upward pull of the cables on the cabin is

options.text_md: greater than the weight, because the cabin is moving upward
equal to the weight of the cabin and passengers, because the net force on it is zero
less than the weight, because the cabin does not accelerate
zero, because the cabin moves with uniform velocity

questions.solution_md: Uniform velocity in a straight line means zero acceleration, hence zero net force (first law). The upward pull balances the downward weight; it is not zero and not greater.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (b)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: The momentum of a trolley changes from 3 kg m s⁻¹ to 11 kg m s⁻¹ in 0.5 s under a steady force along its path. The force on the trolley is
questions.solution_md: The force equals the rate of change of momentum: F = Δp/Δt = (11 − 3)/0.5 = 16 N. Using Δp alone leaves out the division by time.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A steady force of 1 N acts on a body of mass 250 g on a smooth horizontal surface. The acceleration of the body is
questions.solution_md: The mass is 0.25 kg, so a = F/m = 1/0.25 = 4 m s⁻². Using 250 for the mass in grams gives a wrong value; the newton is defined with the mass in kg.

marking_scheme.step: a = F/m = 1/0.25 = 4 m s⁻² (mass converted to kg) (a)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: Two forces of 6 N due east and 8 N due north act together on a 2.5 kg puck on smooth ice. The magnitude of the acceleration of the puck is
questions.solution_md: The components of acceleration are a_x = 6/2.5 = 2.4 m s⁻² and a_y = 8/2.5 = 3.2 m s⁻². Since the forces are at right angles, a = √(2.4² + 3.2²) = 4 m s⁻². Adding the magnitudes of the forces directly is wrong because they are perpendicular.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A proton in an accelerator is pushed by a steady force to speeds close to the speed of light. The force that is needed for a given small increase in speed becomes larger and larger because

options.text_md: the measured mass of the proton increases without limit as its speed approaches the speed of light
the mass of the proton decreases, so it resists the force more strongly
the force of gravity on the proton rises with its speed
the momentum of the proton stays constant while its speed rises

questions.solution_md: Close to the speed of light the measured mass increases without limit, so a given force changes the speed less and less and no body can reach c. F = ma with a constant mass fails there; the law F = dp/dt still holds.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (a)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: Which of the following pairs of quantities has the same dimensions?
questions.solution_md: Impulse is force × time, [M L T⁻²][T] = [M L T⁻¹], the dimensions of momentum (equivalently N s = kg m s⁻¹). Force and kinetic energy have different dimensions from momentum.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (c)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A fielder draws his hands back while catching a fast cricket ball. This reduces the average force on his hands because

options.text_md: the change of momentum of the ball becomes smaller when the hands move back
the impulse on the ball becomes smaller because the hands move back with it
the mass of the ball decreases when it touches the moving hands
the ball takes longer to stop, while its change of momentum stays the same

questions.solution_md: The ball must lose all of its momentum, so Δp is fixed whatever the fielder does. The average force is Δp/Δt, so a longer stopping time gives a smaller force.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (d)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A 0.06 kg ball hits the floor at 5 m s⁻¹ and rebounds vertically upward at 3 m s⁻¹. The magnitude of the impulse given to the ball by the floor is
questions.solution_md: Take upward as positive. The velocity changes from −5 to +3 m s⁻¹, a change of 8 m s⁻¹. The impulse is Δp = 0.06 × 8 = 0.48 N s. Subtracting the speeds instead of adding them ignores the reversal of direction.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: The force on a body rises uniformly from zero to 40 N in 0.1 s and then drops to zero at once. The impulse given to the body is
questions.solution_md: The impulse is the area under the force–time graph, a triangle of base 0.1 s and height 40 N: ½ × 0.1 × 40 = 2 N s. Using the full rectangle 40 × 0.1 counts the force as if it stayed at its peak.

marking_scheme.step: Impulse = area of the triangle = ½ × 0.1 × 40 = 2 N s (b)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A 3 kg rifle fires a bullet of mass 15 g with a muzzle speed of 300 m s⁻¹. The recoil speed of the rifle is
questions.solution_md: Before firing the momentum is zero, so MV = mv in magnitude. With m = 0.015 kg (not 15), V = 0.015 × 300/3 = 1.5 m s⁻¹.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A stationary shell explodes into two fragments whose masses are in the ratio 1 : 3. Immediately after the explosion, the ratio of the kinetic energy of the lighter fragment to that of the heavier fragment is
questions.solution_md: The momenta of the fragments are equal and opposite, p. The kinetic energy is p²/2m, so the energies are in the inverse ratio of the masses: lighter : heavier = 3 : 1. The lighter piece carries more energy.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (c)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A rocket in deep space ejects hot gas backward and accelerates forward. Which statement explains this correctly?

options.text_md: The gas pushes against the empty space around it and the space pushes the rocket forward
The forward force on the rocket cancels the backward force on the gas, so the rocket is left with a net forward force
Momentum is not conserved in space, so the rocket gains forward momentum from nowhere at all
The rocket pushes the gas backward and the gas pushes the rocket forward with an equal force; the two forces act on different bodies

questions.solution_md: The two forces are an action–reaction pair: equal and opposite and acting on different bodies, so they do not cancel. In terms of momentum, the backward momentum of the gas is balanced by the forward momentum of the rocket; the total stays zero.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (d)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A wooden box slides down a smooth inclined plane. Which one of the following lists all the forces to be drawn in its free-body diagram?

options.text_md: Its weight and the normal reaction of the plane
Its weight, the normal reaction and a force down the slope
Its weight, the normal reaction and the force of its motion
Its weight, the normal reaction and the reaction to its weight

questions.solution_md: A free-body diagram shows only the forces acting on the box: the weight (Earth’s pull) and the normal reaction (contact with the plane). The “force down the slope” is a component of the weight, not an extra force; the reaction to the weight acts on the Earth, not on the box.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (a)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A 4 kg block on a smooth horizontal table is joined by a light string over a smooth pulley at the edge to a 1 kg mass hanging freely. Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², the acceleration of the blocks is
questions.solution_md: Only the weight of the hanging mass pulls the whole system of mass 5 kg: a = m₂g/(m₁ + m₂) = 1 × 9.8/5 = 1.96 m s⁻². The acceleration is not g, because the string also has to drag the block on the table.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: Masses of 7 kg and 5 kg hang from the two ends of a light string passing over a smooth fixed pulley. Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², the acceleration of the masses is
questions.solution_md: The net driving force is the difference of the weights, (m₁ − m₂)g, and the mass that has to be accelerated is m₁ + m₂: a = 2 × 9.8/12 = 1.63 m s⁻².

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A horizontal force of 24 N pushes a 5 kg block which is in contact with a 3 kg block on a smooth floor, the 5 kg block being behind. The force exerted by the 5 kg block on the 3 kg block is
questions.solution_md: Both blocks accelerate together at a = 24/(5 + 3) = 3 m s⁻². The only horizontal force on the front block is the contact force, so it equals 3 × 3 = 9 N, much less than the push of 24 N.

marking_scheme.step: a = 24/8 = 3 m s⁻²; contact force = 3 × 3 = 9 N (c)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A 60 kg person stands on a weighing machine in a lift that is accelerating downward at 2 m s⁻². Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², the machine reads a force of
questions.solution_md: Taking downward as positive, mg − N = ma, so N = m(g − a) = 60 × 7.8 = 468 N, which is less than the true weight 588 N. The reading would be 708 N for an upward acceleration.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: Three forces act at a point on a particle. For which set of magnitudes can the particle be in equilibrium?
questions.solution_md: Three concurrent forces balance only if they can form a closed triangle, so each must be less than the sum of the other two. 7 + 9 = 16 > 15, so 7, 9 and 15 can; in the other sets the largest force is more than the sum of the other two.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (b)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: Three coplanar forces that are not parallel keep a rigid body in equilibrium. Which statement must be true?

options.text_md: The three forces are equal in magnitude
Their lines of action meet at one point, and their vector sum is zero
The three forces make angles of 120° with each other, whatever their magnitudes
The lines of action of the three forces are parallel to one another

questions.solution_md: The vector sum must be zero for no translation. If the lines of action did not meet at a point, the torque about the point where two of them meet would come from the third force alone and could not vanish. So the lines are concurrent; the magnitudes may differ.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (b)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A signboard of weight 80 N hangs from a knot supported by two ropes that make 30° and 60° with the horizontal beam above. The tension in the rope that makes 60° with the beam is
questions.solution_md: The two ropes are at right angles (30° + 60° = 90°). Resolving horizontally and vertically gives T = W cos 30° = 69.3 N for the rope at 60° to the beam (the steeper rope carries more of the weight) and W cos 60° = 40 N for the flatter rope.

marking_scheme.step: Lami or resolving: the rope at 60° carries T = W cos 30° = 69.3 N (d)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A uniform ladder rests with its foot on rough ground and its upper end against a smooth vertical wall. The force exerted by the wall on the ladder is

options.text_md: along the length of the ladder
horizontal, away from the wall, and balanced by a horizontal force at the foot
vertically upward, balancing the weight of the ladder
zero, because the wall is smooth

questions.solution_md: A smooth surface exerts only a normal reaction, perpendicular to itself: here horizontal and away from the wall. Nothing else on the ladder has a horizontal component except the force at the floor, which must therefore balance it.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (b)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A uniform ladder leans against a smooth vertical wall. Its foot is moved outward so that its angle with the floor falls from 60° to 30°. The reaction of the wall on the ladder becomes
questions.solution_md: Taking torques about the foot, N_w = (W/2) cot θ. Hence the ratio is cot 30°/cot 60° = 1.73/0.577 = 3: a less steep ladder pushes harder on the wall.

marking_scheme.step: N_w = (W/2) cot θ: cot 30°/cot 60° = 3 (a)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A passenger standing in a train is thrown backward when the train starts suddenly.

**Reason (R):** The body of the passenger tends to remain at rest, while the floor of the train moves forward.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: the passenger seems to move backward relative to the train. R is true and is exactly the reason: inertia of rest keeps the body at rest while the feet are carried forward with the floor.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (a)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The tension in a light string passing over a smooth pulley is the same on both sides of the pulley.

**Reason (R):** In an Atwood machine with unequal masses, the tension in the string is greater than the weight of the lighter mass.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: a light string over a smooth pulley transmits the same tension. R is also true, since the lighter mass accelerates upward and T − m₂g = m₂a > 0. But R does not explain A; equal tension follows from the string and pulley being massless and frictionless.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (b)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Of two bodies with the same kinetic energy, the heavier has the greater momentum.

**Reason (R):** The momentum of a body does not depend on its mass.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: p = √(2mK), so for the same K the larger mass has the larger momentum. R is false: p = mv depends on the mass directly.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (c)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A ladder resting on a smooth wall can be in equilibrium on a floor that exerts only a vertical force on its foot.

**Reason (R):** The reaction of a smooth wall on the ladder is perpendicular to the wall.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: the wall reaction is horizontal, so for no net horizontal force the floor must exert a horizontal force on the foot as well. R is true, but it is the reason why a horizontal floor force is required, not why it can be absent.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (d)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A person in a lift that accelerates upward reads more than the true weight on a weighing machine.

**Reason (R):** When the lift accelerates upward, the net force on the person is upward, so the normal reaction of the floor exceeds the weight.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: N = m(g + a) > mg. R is true and explains it: the net force N − mg = ma is upward, which needs the normal reaction (the reading) to be larger than the weight.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (a)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The third law can be obtained from the conservation of momentum for two bodies that interact only with each other.

**Reason (R):** A pair of bodies that interact only with each other has a net external force on it.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: with p_A + p_B constant, dp_A/dt = −dp_B/dt, so the two forces are equal and opposite. R is false: such a pair is an isolated system, with no net external force; that is why its total momentum is conserved.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (c)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: True or false? The weight of a book lying on a table and the normal reaction of the table on the book form an action–reaction pair of the third law.
questions.solution_md: False. Both forces act on the same body, the book. The reaction to the weight is the book’s pull on the Earth; the reaction to the normal reaction is the book’s push on the table.

marking_scheme.step: False, with the correction

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: True or false? Three parallel coplanar forces can keep a rigid body in equilibrium.
questions.solution_md: True. For example, a plank resting on two supports with a load between them: the middle force acts opposite to the other two, and both the force sum and the torque sum can be zero.

marking_scheme.step: True

questions.stem_md: The impulse of a force acting on a body is equal to the change in ___ of the body.
questions.solution_md: From F = Δp/Δt, the impulse FΔt equals the change in **momentum**.

marking_scheme.step: Writes "momentum"

questions.stem_md: A uniform ladder of length 5 m and mass 15 kg rests against a smooth wall, making 60° with the level floor. A painter of mass 60 kg stands on it at a point 3 m from its foot, measured along the ladder. Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², find the reaction of the wall on the ladder, in N.

marking_scheme.step: Torque about the foot: N_w L sin θ = mg (L/2) cos θ + Mg d cos θ

questions.stem_md: State Newton’s first law of motion. A cyclist stops pedalling on a level road and slowly comes to rest. Does this contradict the law?

answer.model_answer_md: A body continues in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless a net external force acts on it. questions.stem_md: Why is a loaded handcart harder to start moving, and harder to stop, than the same cart when it is empty? Answer in terms of inertia and mass.

answer.model_answer_md: Inertia is the resistance of a body to a change in its state of rest or of motion, and its measure is the mass. The loaded cart has a larger mass and therefore a larger inertia, so the same force produces a smaller change in velocity, both in starting and in stopping it.

questions.solution_md: More mass means more inertia, so less acceleration for the same force.

marking_scheme.step: Inertia is resistance to a change of state, measured by mass
The loaded cart has more mass, so a given force gives a smaller change of velocity when starting or stopping

questions.stem_md: Using the second law, define the newton and show that 1 N is the same as 1 kg m s⁻².

answer.model_answer_md: One newton is the force which gives a body of mass one kilogram an acceleration of one metre per second squared. From $F = ma$, $1\ \text{N} = (1\ \text{kg})(1\ \text{m s}^{-2}) = 1\ \text{kg m s}^{-2}$, so the newton is a derived unit built from the base units kilogram, metre and second.

questions.stem_md: A girl pulls a 20 kg sled on smooth ice with a rope making 30° with the horizontal, the force in the rope being 80 N. Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², find the acceleration of the sled and the normal reaction on it.

marking_scheme.step: The change of momentum, hence the impulse, is the same in both landings

questions.stem_md: State the law of conservation of linear momentum and the condition under which it holds for a system of colliding bodies.

answer.model_answer_md: The total linear momentum of a system stays constant, in magnitude and direction, if no net external force acts on it. questions.solution_md: Law and condition (no net external force).

Condition: no net external force; internal forces only redistribute momentum

answer.model_answer_md: An action–reaction pair acts on two different bodies. The weight and the normal reaction both act on the same body, the book, and they only happen to balance. The reaction to the weight of the book is the gravitational pull of the book on the Earth, directed upward.

questions.solution_md: Both forces act on the book; the pair partner acts on the Earth.

marking_scheme.step: Both forces act on the same body (the book), but a third-law pair acts on different bodies

questions.stem_md: A block rests on a smooth horizontal table and is pulled by a horizontal light string that passes over a pulley at the edge of the table. List the forces in the free-body diagram of the block, giving the direction of each.

answer.model_answer_md: Three forces act on the block. Its weight mg acts vertically downward. questions.solution_md: Weight, normal reaction, tension: nothing else.

questions.solution_md: Massless string and frictionless pulley.

marking_scheme.step: Massless string: net force on any element is zero, so the tension is the same along it

questions.stem_md: A 55 kg person stands on a weighing machine in a lift. Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², find the reading of the machine (in newtons) when the lift accelerates downward at 1.2 m s⁻², and when it moves upward at constant velocity.

answer.model_answer_md: Apply the second law to the person, taking downward as positive: $mg - N = ma$, so $N = m(g - a) = 55 \times (9.8 - 1.2) = 473\ \text{N}$ while the lift accelerates downward. At constant velocity the acceleration is zero, so $N = mg = 55 \times 9.8 = 539\ \text{N}$, which is the true weight of the person.

questions.solution_md: N = m(g − a) when accelerating down; N = mg at constant velocity.

marking_scheme.step: Accelerating down: N = m(g − a) = 473 N
Constant velocity: N = mg = 539 N

answer.model_answer_md: First, the vector sum of all the forces on the body must be zero, $\sum\vec{F} = 0$, so that it has no translational acceleration. Second, the sum of the torques of the forces about any point must be zero, so that the body has no angular acceleration and does not start to turn.

questions.solution_md: Zero resultant force and zero resultant torque.

marking_scheme.step: Resultant force is zero (no translational acceleration)
Resultant torque about any point is zero (no rotation)

questions.stem_md: State Lami’s theorem for three concurrent forces in equilibrium, and say which angle goes with each force in the ratio.

answer.model_answer_md: If three concurrent forces keep a particle in equilibrium, each force is proportional to the sine of the angle between the other two: $\dfrac{F_1}{\sin\alpha} = \dfrac{F_2}{\sin\beta} = \dfrac{F_3}{\sin\gamma}$. Here $\alpha$ lies between $F_2$ and $F_3$, $\beta$ between $F_3$ and $F_1$, and $\gamma$ between $F_1$ and $F_2$.

questions.solution_md: Each force over the sine of the angle opposite it, between the other two.

marking_scheme.step: Each force is proportional to the sine of the angle between the other two
F₁/sin α = F₂/sin β = F₃/sin γ with α between F₂ and F₃ and so on

questions.stem_md: Starting from the second law in the form F = dp/dt, derive F = ma for a body of constant mass, and use it to define the newton.

answer.model_answer_md: The second law states that the net force equals the rate of change of momentum, $F = \dfrac{dp}{dt}$. For a body of constant mass $p = mv$, and the constant $m$ can be taken outside the derivative, so $F = \dfrac{d(mv)}{dt} = m\dfrac{dv}{dt} = ma$, because $\dfrac{dv}{dt}$ is the acceleration. One newton is then the force that gives a mass of one kilogram an acceleration of one metre per second squared.

questions.solution_md: Put p = mv, take m outside, then define the unit.

marking_scheme.step: F = dp/dt with p = mv
m is constant: F = m dv/dt = ma
1 N = force giving 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s⁻²

questions.stem_md: A footballer kicks a stationary 0.4 kg ball, which leaves the boot at 18 m s⁻¹. The contact lasts 0.01 s. Show that the impulse of the force equals the change in momentum, and find the impulse and the average force.

answer.model_answer_md: For a constant force, $F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$, so the impulse $F\Delta t = \Delta p$, the change in momentum of the body. The ball starts from rest, so its change in momentum is its final momentum, and $\Delta p = mv - 0 = 0.4 \times 18 = 7.2\ \text{N s}$, which is the impulse. The average force is $F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{7.2}{0.01} = 720\ \text{N}$.

questions.solution_md: Impulse = change in momentum; then divide by the contact time.

marking_scheme.step: Impulse FΔt = Δp from F = Δp/Δt
Impulse = 0.4 × 18 = 7.2 N s

questions.stem_md: Starting from the second law, show that the total linear momentum of an isolated system of two particles is constant.

answer.model_answer_md: For the system of two particles with momenta $\vec{p}_1$ and $\vec{p}_2$, the second law gives the net external force as the rate of change of the total momentum, $\vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = \dfrac{d(\vec{p}_1 + \vec{p}_2)}{dt}$. In an isolated system no external force acts, so $\vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = 0$. Hence $\dfrac{d\vec{P}}{dt} = 0$, and $\vec{P} = \vec{p}_1 + \vec{p}_2$ is constant.

questions.solution_md: Second law for the system with zero external force.

marking_scheme.step: Second law for the system: F_ext = d(p₁ + p₂)/dt
Isolated system: F_ext = 0, so dP/dt = 0
Therefore P = p₁ + p₂ is constant (conserved)

questions.stem_md: Two bodies A and B interact only with each other. Using the conservation of linear momentum, show that the force on A due to B is equal and opposite to the force on B due to A.

answer.model_answer_md: The pair is isolated, so the total momentum is constant, $\vec{p}_A + \vec{p}_B = \text{constant}$. Differentiating with time gives $\dfrac{d\vec{p}_A}{dt} + \dfrac{d\vec{p}_B}{dt} = 0$. By the second law each rate of change of momentum is the force on that body, so $\vec{F}_{\text{on A}} = -\vec{F}_{\text{on B}}$. These are equal and opposite, acting on different bodies: Newton's third law.

questions.solution_md: Differentiate p_A + p_B = constant and read off the forces.

marking_scheme.step: Isolated pair: p_A + p_B = constant
Differentiate: dp_A/dt = −dp_B/dt
By the second law F on A = −F on B: the third law

questions.stem_md: A gun of mass M fires a bullet of mass m with velocity v. Derive the recoil velocity of the gun and show that the kinetic energy of the gun is smaller than that of the bullet by the factor m/M.

answer.model_answer_md: Before firing the total momentum is zero. The forces between gun and bullet are internal, so the momentum is conserved and stays zero: $0 = mv + MV$ and $V = -\dfrac{m}{M}v$. The gun recoils opposite to the bullet. For the energies, the kinetic energy of the gun is $\tfrac{1}{2}MV^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}M\dfrac{m^2v^2}{M^2} = \dfrac{m}{M}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\right)$, which is the fraction $\dfrac{m}{M}$ of the bullet's kinetic energy.

questions.solution_md: Conserve momentum from rest, then substitute V into the energy.

marking_scheme.step: 0 = mv + MV by conservation of momentum
V = −mv/M, opposite to the bullet
K_gun = ½MV² = (m/M)(½mv²), so K_gun/K_bullet = m/M

questions.stem_md: Masses m₁ and m₂ (m₁ > m₂) hang from the ends of a light string passing over a smooth pulley. Derive expressions for the acceleration of the masses and for the tension in the string.

answer.model_answer_md: On each mass only its weight and the tension of the string act. Both masses have acceleration $a$, $m_1$ downward and $m_2$ upward, and the string has the same tension $T$. Applying the second law to each mass, for $m_1$: $m_1g - T = m_1a$. For $m_2$: $T - m_2g = m_2a$. Adding eliminates $T$: $a = \dfrac{(m_1 - m_2)g}{m_1 + m_2}$. Substituting in the second equation, $T = m_2(g + a) = \dfrac{2m_1m_2g}{m_1 + m_2}$.

questions.solution_md: One equation for each mass; add, then substitute back.

marking_scheme.step: m₁g − T = m₁a and T − m₂g = m₂a (same a and T)
Adding: a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂)
T = m₂(g + a) = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂)

answer.model_answer_md: The forces on the person are the weight $mg$ downward and the normal reaction $N$ of the floor upward; $N$ is what the machine reads. Taking upward as positive, $N - mg = ma$, so the apparent weight is $N = m(g + a)$, greater than $mg$. For a downward acceleration $a$ the same working gives $N = m(g - a)$, so for $a = g$ the reading is zero.

questions.solution_md: Newton’s second law for the person with upward positive.

marking_scheme.step: Forces: weight mg down, N up; N − mg = ma
N = m(g + a): apparent weight is larger for an upward acceleration
Downward acceleration: N = m(g − a), which is zero for a = g

questions.stem_md: A force F pushes a block of mass m₁ that is in contact with a block of mass m₂ on a smooth floor, m₁ being behind. Derive expressions for the acceleration and for the force exerted by m₁ on m₂.

answer.model_answer_md: The blocks move together, so treat them as one body of mass $m_1 + m_2$ acted on by $F$: $a = \dfrac{F}{m_1 + m_2}$. The only horizontal force on $m_2$ is the contact force $F_c$ from $m_1$, so $F_c = m_2a = \dfrac{m_2}{m_1 + m_2}F$. By the third law $m_2$ pushes back on $m_1$ with an equal force, so for $m_1$, $F - F_c = m_1a$.

questions.solution_md: Whole system for a, then the front block alone for the contact force.

marking_scheme.step: Both blocks together: F = (m₁ + m₂)a, a = F/(m₁ + m₂)
Front block alone: contact force F_c = m₂a

questions.stem_md: State Lami’s theorem and prove it from the triangle of forces.

answer.model_answer_md: If three concurrent forces $F_1$, $F_2$, $F_3$ are in equilibrium, each is proportional to the sine of the angle between the other two. By the triangle law the forces form a closed triangle, whose sides are proportional to the forces. The sine rule says each side is proportional to the sine of the opposite angle, which is the supplement of the angle between the other two forces, with the same sine. Hence $\dfrac{F_1}{\sin\alpha} = \dfrac{F_2}{\sin\beta} = \dfrac{F_3}{\sin\gamma}$.

questions.solution_md: Sine rule on the closed force triangle; supplementary angles have equal sines.

marking_scheme.step: Statement: each force is proportional to the sine of the angle between the other two
The forces form a closed triangle (triangle law); apply the sine rule to it
The angle opposite a side is the supplement of the angle between the other forces, with the same sine: F₁/sin α = F₂/sin β = F₃/sin γ

questions.stem_md: A uniform ladder rests with its foot on the ground and its top against a smooth wall. Name the forces on the ladder, give the direction of each, and explain why the ground must exert a horizontal force on the foot.

marking_scheme.step: Weight at the middle (down); wall reaction at the top, horizontal and away from the wall
At the foot: normal reaction upward and a horizontal force towards the wall

questions.stem_md: Forces of 30 N due east and 40 N due north act on a particle together with a third force F, and the particle stays in equilibrium. Find the magnitude and direction of F.

questions.stem_md: A block of mass m₁ lies on a smooth horizontal table and is joined by a light string over a smooth pulley to a mass m₂ hanging freely. Derive the acceleration of the system and the tension in the string.

marking_scheme.step: T = m₁a for the block on the table; m₂g − T = m₂a for the hanging mass
Adding: a = m₂g/(m₁ + m₂)

questions.stem_md: A block of mass 8 kg slides down a smooth plane inclined at 25° to the horizontal. Name the forces on it, and find its acceleration and the normal reaction. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².

questions.stem_md: Show that three non-parallel coplanar forces can keep a rigid body in equilibrium only if their lines of action meet at one point.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Impulse is the product of a force and the time for which it acts. From the second law $F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$, so $F\,\Delta t = \Delta p$: the impulse equals the change in momentum.

(b) The ball reverses its direction, so the two speeds add. (i) Taking the outgoing direction as positive, $J = m(v - u) = 0.17\,(30 + 25) = 9.35\ \text{N s}$. (ii) $F = \dfrac{J}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{9.35}{0.005} = 1870\ \text{N}$. (iii) $F = \dfrac{0.17 \times 25}{0.04} = 106.25\ \text{N}$, much smaller than in (ii) because the same change of momentum is spread over a longer time, and the ball is merely stopped, not reversed.

questions.solution_md: Reverse the direction in (i); a longer time in (iii) gives a smaller force.

marking_scheme.step: Impulse = force × time of action
F Δt = Δp from F = Δp/Δt

questions.stem_md: (a) Derive the recoil velocity of a gun of mass M that fires a bullet of mass m with velocity v. [2] (b) A 6 kg gun fires a 40 g shell at 250 m s⁻¹. Find (i) the recoil speed of the gun [1], and (ii) the average force needed to bring the gun to rest in 0.25 s. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Gun and bullet are at rest before firing, so the total momentum is zero, and it stays zero because the explosion uses only internal forces. Hence $0 = mv + MV$, so $V = -\dfrac{m}{M}v$: the gun recoils in the direction opposite to the bullet, slowly because $M$ is much larger than $m$.

(b) The mass of the shell must be taken in kilograms. (i) $V = \dfrac{mv}{M} =\dfrac{0.04 \times 250}{6} = 1.67\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. (ii) The impulse needed is the momentum of the gun, so $F = \dfrac{MV}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{6 \times 1.667}{0.25} = 40\ \text{N}$.

questions.solution_md: Conservation of momentum from rest; then stop the gun with an impulse.

marking_scheme.step: Total momentum zero before and after (internal forces only): 0 = mv + MV
V = −mv/M: opposite direction and small because M ≫ m
Impulse to stop the gun = MV, F = MV/Δt

questions.stem_md: (a) Derive the law of conservation of linear momentum for an isolated system of two bodies, starting from Newton’s second law. [2] (b) Hence show that Newton’s third law follows from the conservation of momentum, and explain why the two forces of an action–reaction pair do not cancel each other. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) For a system, the net external force equals the rate of change of the total momentum, $\vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = \dfrac{d\vec{P}}{dt}$ with $\vec{P} = \vec{p}_1 + \vec{p}_2$. In an isolated system $\vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = 0$, so $\dfrac{d\vec{P}}{dt} = 0$ and the total momentum is constant.

(b) For two bodies A and B interacting only with each other, $\vec{p}_A + \vec{p}_B$ is constant, so $\dfrac{d\vec{p}_A}{dt} = -\dfrac{d\vec{p}_B}{dt}$. By the second law these are the forces on A and on B: $\vec{F}_{\text{on A}} = -\vec{F}_{\text{on B}}$, the third law. They do not cancel because they act on different bodies.

questions.solution_md: Second law for the system, then differentiate the conserved total.

marking_scheme.step: Second law for the system: F_ext = dP/dt
Isolated: F_ext = 0, so P is constant
p_A + p_B constant, so dp_A/dt = −dp_B/dt
F on A = −F on B (third law)
The pair acts on different bodies, so the forces cannot cancel

questions.stem_md: (a) Draw free-body diagrams for two masses m₁ > m₂ hung from a light string over a smooth pulley, and derive expressions for the acceleration and the tension. [3] (b) For m₁ = 9 kg and m₂ = 7 kg released from rest, with g = 9.8 m s⁻², find the acceleration, the tension, and the speed of the masses 2 s after release. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The free-body diagram of each mass shows two forces only: its weight, downward, and the tension of the string, upward. Both masses have the same magnitude of acceleration $a$ and the string has one tension $T$, because it is light and the pulley is smooth. Applying the second law to each, for $m_1$ (down): $m_1g - T = m_1a$. For $m_2$ (up): $T - m_2g = m_2a$. Adding, $a = \dfrac{(m_1 - m_2)g}{m_1 + m_2}$ and $T = \dfrac{2m_1m_2g}{m_1 + m_2}$.

(b) Substituting the masses in kilograms and taking g as 9.8 metres per second squared, $a = \dfrac{(9 - 7)(9.8)}{9 + 7} = 1.225\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, $T = \dfrac{2(9)(7)(9.8)}{9 + 7} = 77.18\ \text{N}$, and $v = at = 1.225 \times 2 = 2.45\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

questions.solution_md: One equation per mass; add; then substitute the numbers.

marking_scheme.step: Free-body diagrams: weight and tension on each mass; same a and T
m₁g − T = m₁a and T − m₂g = m₂a, giving a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂)
T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂)
v = at = 2.45 m s⁻¹

questions.stem_md: (a) A person of mass m stands on a weighing machine in a lift. Derive the reading of the machine when the lift accelerates with acceleration a (i) upward and (ii) downward. [3] (b) A 70 kg person sees the machine read 616 N. Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², find the acceleration of the lift and its direction, and the reading if the lift moved at constant velocity. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The forces on the person are the weight $mg$ downward and the normal reaction $N$ of the floor, upward, which is the reading. (i) For upward acceleration, $N - mg = ma$, so $N = m(g + a)$, more than the weight. (ii) For downward acceleration, $mg - N = ma$, so $N = m(g - a)$, less than the weight.

(b) The reading is below the weight $686\ \text{N}$, so the lift accelerates downward: $70(9.8 - a) = 616$ gives $a = 9.8 - 8.8 = 1\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. At constant velocity the reading is $mg = 686\ \text{N}$.

questions.solution_md: Normal reaction with the sign of the acceleration; the reading is below mg in (b).

marking_scheme.step: Forces: mg down, N up (the reading)
Upward acceleration: N − mg = ma, N = m(g + a)
Downward acceleration: mg − N = ma, N = m(g − a)
Reading 616 N < 686 N: downward, a = 1 m s⁻²
Constant velocity: N = mg = 686 N

questions.stem_md: (a) State the triangle law of forces and Lami’s theorem. [2] (b) A traffic signal of weight 180 N hangs from a knot supported by two cables that make 30° and 45° with the horizontal. Find the tension in each cable. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Triangle law: if three concurrent forces keep a particle in equilibrium, they can be drawn head to tail to form a closed triangle. Lami’s theorem: each of the three forces is proportional to the sine of the angle between the other two.

(b) The angle between the cables is $180^\circ - (30^\circ + 45^\circ) = 105^\circ$, and $\sin105^\circ = \sin75^\circ =0.9659$. For the cable at 30°: $T_1 = \dfrac{W\cos45^\circ}{\sin75^\circ} = 131.8\ \text{N}$. For the cable at 45°: $T_2 = \dfrac{W\cos30^\circ}{\sin75^\circ} = 161.4\ \text{N}$.

questions.solution_md: Lami, or resolve horizontally and vertically.

marking_scheme.step: Triangle law: three concurrent forces in equilibrium form a closed triangle
Lami: each force proportional to the sine of the angle between the other two
sin 75° = 0.9659 from the sum of the two cable angles
T₁ = W cos 45°/sin 75° = 131.8 N
T₂ = W cos 30°/sin 75° = 161.4 N

questions.stem_md: (a) A uniform ladder rests with its foot on rough ground and its top against a smooth vertical wall. Describe, or draw, the forces on the ladder and write the conditions of equilibrium. [2] (b) Derive an expression for the reaction of the wall in terms of the weight W of the ladder and its angle θ with the ground. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The weight $W$ acts down at the centre of the ladder. The smooth wall gives a horizontal reaction $N_w$ at the top. The ground gives a vertical reaction $N_f$ and a horizontal force $F_f$ at the foot. Equilibrium needs $\sum\vec{F} = 0$ and zero total torque.

(b) Vertically $N_f = W$ and horizontally $F_f = N_w$. Take torques about the foot, where the floor forces have no moment. The wall reaction has the arm $L\sin\theta$ and the weight has the arm $\dfrac{L}{2}\cos\theta$, so $N_wL\sin\theta = W\dfrac{L}{2}\cos\theta$ and $N_w = \dfrac{W}{2}\cot\theta$.

questions.solution_md: Torques about the foot remove the unknown floor forces.

marking_scheme.step: Forces: W down at the middle; N_w horizontal at the top; N_f up and F_f horizontal at the foot
Conditions: ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0
N_f = W and F_f = N_w from force balance
Torques about the foot: N_w L sin θ = W (L/2) cos θ
N_w = (W/2) cot θ

questions.stem_md: A uniform ladder of length 4.5 m and mass 12 kg rests against a smooth wall, making 55° with the level floor. A girl of mass 40 kg stands 3 m from the foot, measured along the ladder. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². (a) Find the reaction of the wall. [3] (b) Find the normal reaction and the horizontal force at the floor, and the magnitude of the total floor reaction. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Take torques about the foot, so that the unknown floor forces drop out of the equation. The wall reaction acts at the top. The ladder’s weight acts at its middle, $\dfrac{L}{2} = 2.25$ m along it, and the girl’s weight acts at 3 m. Then $N_w (L\sin55^\circ) = mg\dfrac{L}{2}\cos55^\circ + Mg\,d\cos55^\circ$, that is $N_w \times 3.686 = 151.8 + 674.5$, so $N_w = 224.2\ \text{N}$.

(b) The floor must support the weight of the ladder and the girl together. Vertical balance gives $N_f = (12 + 40)(9.8) = 509.6\ \text{N}$. Horizontal balance gives $F_f = N_w = 224.2\ \text{N}$. The total floor reaction is $\sqrt{509.6^2 + 224.2^2} = 556.7\ \text{N}$.

questions.solution_md: Torques about the foot, then the two force balances.

marking_scheme.step: Torque equation about the foot: N_w L sin θ = mg (L/2) cos θ + Mg d cos θ
Moments 151.8 N m and 674.5 N m; L sin θ = 3.686 m
N_f = 509.6 N and F_f = N_w = 224.2 N
Total floor reaction = 556.7 N
